title: NASA's New Camera Is 300 Megapixels — And It Just Woke Up!
summary: Imagine a camera so powerful it could take a picture of a single star and also a whole galaxy at the same time. NASA just switched on a camera like that in space. It's called the Wide Field Instrument, and it has 300 megapixels. That's about 150 times more pixels than a typical phone camera. The camera is riding on a telescope named Roman. Right now, Roman is flying toward a spot about one million miles from Earth. Before turning the camera on, engineers had to cool it down. They chilled it to minus 225 degrees Fahrenheit — colder than any freezer on Earth. That extreme cold helps the camera see infrared light, which is a kind of heat glow that comes from faraway stars and planets. One picture from this camera will cover a piece of sky bigger than the full moon looks from the ground. That means it can take huge group photos of the universe. Scientists hope to use it to study dark energy, a mysterious force that pushes the universe apart, and to find planets around other stars. The first science pictures should arrive by early 2027. Get ready for some amazing space postcards!
why_it_matters: Big telescopes like this one help answer questions about where our universe came from — and the amazing pictures they send back may show up in your science class or in your own backyard stargazing.

background_read: NASA (the U.S. space agency that sends rockets, astronauts, and telescopes into space) named this telescope after Nancy Grace Roman, an astronomer sometimes called the 'mother of Hubble' for helping plan the famous Hubble Space Telescope.
The telescope will settle at a spot about one million miles from Earth called L2 — the same faraway place where the James Webb Space Telescope orbits.
Space cameras often look for infrared light, because infrared can show warm, faraway objects that our eyes cannot see.

WHAT: They turned on a 300-megapixel camera — about 150 times more pixels than a typical phone camera — after cooling it to minus 225 degrees Fahrenheit.
WHERE: On the telescope named Roman, which is flying toward a spot about one million miles from Earth.
WHY: The camera will take huge 'group photos' of the sky to study dark energy and find planets around other stars, with the first science pictures expected by early 2027.

perspectives.description: They say this camera is a huge step because it can photograph enormous pieces of sky and help solve the mystery of dark energy.
They know the camera must stay super cold and work perfectly a million miles away, where no one can go up to fix it.
Space fans and kids are waiting for the first pictures, hoping for beautiful 'space postcards' that make the universe feel closer.
